# Images reference

Rimsky publishes fifteen images to `docker.io/rimskyai`: four core images and eleven bundled-service images. Each release pushes every image under two tags — the release version and the floating `latest` tag. A pre-release build pushes the floating `dev` tag instead, so `latest` never moves for a dev build.

This reference names each image, what it runs, the commands it accepts, the paths it reads and writes, the ports it opens, and — for the executor images — the attributes it reads from a node and the attributes it writes back.

## Read this first: the images are single-architecture

Every published image carries one platform, `linux/arm64`. None carries `linux/amd64`, and none is a multi-platform index over both. An operator on Apple silicon or Graviton can pull and run. An operator on x86-64 gets no runnable image and finds out at `docker run`.

The CLI is the exception, and it is not an image. Rimsky ships the CLI as release archives covering Linux and macOS on both amd64 and arm64.

## Core images

### `rimsky`

The orchestrator. The image carries all four role binaries — scheduler, supervisor, control API, and migrate — plus the entrypoint that selects among them, and the `rimsky` CLI binary.

The entrypoint reads its single command argument and accepts four forms.

| Command | What the container runs |
| --- | --- |
| *(no command)* | All three roles — scheduler, supervisor, control API — in one process |
| `rimsky-scheduler` | The scheduler role only, as a child process |
| `rimsky-supervisor` | The supervisor role only, as a child process |
| `rimsky-control-api` | The control API role only, as a child process |

Any other argument, and any invocation with more than one argument, exits non-zero with an error naming the valid roles.

The entrypoint runs schema migrations synchronously before the roles start, but only when the invocation owns the migration. The no-command form always owns it. A single-role container owns it only when the role is `rimsky-control-api`, so a three-container split migrates exactly once. Set `RIMSKY_ENTRYPOINT_MIGRATE=1` to force the step, or `=0` to skip it — a dedicated init container uses the first, and role containers behind it use the second. Any other non-empty value is a startup error naming the value.

The image expects two configuration files and neither is baked in. Mount both.

| Path | What reads it |
| --- | --- |
| `/etc/rimsky/rimsky.yml` | The default of `RIMSKY_CONFIG` — persistence, claim producers, executors, publishers, named locks |
| `/etc/rimsky/supervisor-config.yml` | The default of `RIMSKY_SUPERVISOR_CONFIG` — concurrency, poll intervals, the callback listener |
| `/var/lib/rimsky` | A declared volume; the SQLite backend writes its database here |

The supervisor refuses to start when its configuration file is missing. It also refuses when the callback listener binds a wildcard address and no advertise host is set, rather than stamping an unreachable callback URL into dispatches. Set `callback.advertise_host` in the supervisor configuration, or `RIMSKY_SUPERVISOR_CALLBACK_ADVERTISE_HOST`, to a hostname the executors can reach.

The image exposes 8080 and runs as an unprivileged user. The control API binds `127.0.0.1` by default; set `RIMSKY_CONTROL_API_HOST` to reach it from outside the container.

Configuration values reach the container through the mounted file, not through per-key environment variables. The loader expands `${VAR}` references inside the YAML from the container's environment, and rejects unknown keys outright. A variable invented to match a configuration key — a persistence driver, a SQLite path, an executor endpoint — changes nothing and is not refused; the container starts on the unchanged file. Only the enumerated `RIMSKY_*` variables configure a deployment directly.

**The single-process form registers services the split form does not.** Running the image with no command registers four executors and two claim producers inside the orchestrator process: `claude-agent`, `http-node`, `verifier-http`, `verifier-shape-checks`, `claim-producer-filesystem`, and `claim-producer-postgres`. Each registers only when its own configuration is present — a claim producer when its configuration path is set, the Claude executor when a credential is present. The three single-role containers register none of them. A split deployment that wants those six services runs their images.

### `rimsky-all-in-one`

The `rimsky` image with zero-configuration SQLite defaults baked in, for local development. It runs out of the box:

```
docker run -p 8080:8080 rimskyai/rimsky-all-in-one
```

It builds from the `rimsky` image and inherits the entrypoint, the volume, the configuration paths, and the four commands. Three things differ. It bakes `/etc/rimsky/rimsky.yml` with the SQLite driver pointed at `/var/lib/rimsky/state.db`, and no claim producers, executors, or publishers wired in. It bakes `/etc/rimsky/supervisor-config.yml` with concurrency 8 and the async-callback listener on port 9100, bound to `0.0.0.0` and advertising `127.0.0.1`. It sets `RIMSKY_CONTROL_API_HOST=0.0.0.0` so a published port reaches the control API.

Combined with anonymous mode — no API keys — that last default exposes an unauthenticated admin API on every interface. The image is for local development. A deployed instance runs the `rimsky` image with the Postgres driver and its own mounted configuration.

Mounting a host directory at `/var/lib/rimsky` carries state across container replacement. Templates, instances, event history, messages, and per-node run counts all come back under the same identifiers after the container is destroyed and a fresh one starts over the same directory. A container started with nothing mounted comes up with no templates and no instances.

Override either baked file by mounting your own at the same path:

```
docker run -v ./my-rimsky.yml:/etc/rimsky/rimsky.yml:ro rimskyai/rimsky-all-in-one
```

### `rimsky-host-agent-proxy`

The stack-side half of the host-agent pair. A developer's host agent dials this proxy, and the proxy relays spawn, dispatch, and reap requests out to that developer's machine.

The proxy opens one or two listeners. The agent-facing gRPC listener carries the host-agent protocol on `RIMSKY_PROXY_GRPC_PORT`, default 9090. Under `RIMSKY_PEER_AUTH=mtls` the proxy enrolls with the deployment's certificate authority, renews its own leaf, and moves the peer-service protocols — executor, claim producer, lifecycle subscriber, and their observability siblings — onto a second listener at `RIMSKY_PROXY_PEER_GRPC_PORT`, default 9091, which requires client certificates. Without mTLS both sets share the agent-facing port.

`RIMSKY_CONTROL_API_URL` is mandatory in practice. The proxy verifies each agent's registration key against the control API and routes by the key identity the control API reports. With no control API URL the proxy starts and then refuses every registration, so no agent can attach.

`RIMSKY_PROXY_TLS_CERT` and `RIMSKY_PROXY_TLS_KEY` set the agent-facing listener's server TLS. `RIMSKY_CONTROL_API_TOKEN` authenticates the proxy's own cache-miss lookups against the control API, and `RIMSKY_CONTROL_API_CA` supplies a CA bundle for an HTTPS control API — a CA path set against a non-HTTPS URL is a startup error.

### `rimsky-conformance`

The protocol conformance runners, for a third party proving an implementation against rimsky's protocols. The image ships the `rimsky` binary and sets no entrypoint, so name the full command:

```
docker run rimskyai/rimsky-conformance \
  rimsky conformance executor --endpoint grpc://host:9091 --transport grpc
```

Eight subcommands ship: `executor`, `claim-producer`, `publisher`, `validation`, `data-processing`, `blob-backend`, `lifecycle-subscriber`, and `probe`. Two of those cover something other than a protocol. The two observability protocols have no subcommand of their own; `--check-observability` on the executor and claim-producer subcommands runs them. The host-agent protocol has no runner at all, so an implementation of it has nothing to prove itself against.

Every subcommand takes `--endpoint` and `--transport`. Only `claim-producer` accepts `--transport http`; the rest accept `grpc` alone and exit 2 on anything else.

Read the runner's output, not its status. No subcommand accepts a JSON flag, so a CI job parses the printed check rows and the closing `N/M checks failed` line as text. Three exit codes exist and one covers every runtime outcome: 0 for a conforming implementation, 1 for both a failed check and an endpoint that was never reached, 2 for a usage error. The status alone cannot tell a failing implementation from an unreachable one.

## Bundled service images

Eleven images ship the consumption-side services. Six of them — the two claim producers and the four executors — also run inside the single-process `rimsky` and `rimsky-all-in-one` containers, so a local stack often needs none of them. The four sensors and the OpenLineage subscriber run only as their own containers.

### Claim producers

**`rimsky-claim-producer-filesystem`** serves claims over directories. It requires `RIMSKY_CLAIM_PRODUCER_FILESYSTEM_CONFIG`, a path to a YAML file, and exits at startup naming that variable when it is unset. The configuration takes `root`, `host`, `grpc_port`, `http_port`, `http_bridge_url`, `admin_port`, `sweep_interval_seconds`, `enable_lifecycle`, `ledger_max_records`, and a `pick_policies` map whose entries take `root`, `folder_pattern`, `on_commit`, `on_give_up`, `visibility_timeout_seconds`, and `sync_strategy`. It listens on 9100 for gRPC and 9110 for the HTTP bridge, and binds `0.0.0.0` unless `host` says otherwise. A pick policy with `sync_strategy: explicit` needs an admin listener, so `admin_port` becomes required — and that combination cannot run bundled inside the orchestrator process, which never binds one.

**`rimsky-claim-producer-postgres`** serves claims over Postgres tables. It requires `RIMSKY_CLAIM_PRODUCER_POSTGRES_CONFIG`. The configuration takes `connection`, `write_semantics` (`sync`, `staged_async`, `blocking_async`, or `read_only`; default `staged_async`), the same host and port keys, `sweep_interval_seconds`, `enable_lifecycle`, `enable_executor`, `ledger_max_records`, a `pick_policies` map (`items_table`, `on_commit`, `on_give_up`, `visibility_timeout_seconds`), and a `partition_policies` map (`items_table`, `select`, `where`, `params_schema.properties`, `limit`). It listens on 9101 for gRPC and 9111 for the HTTP bridge, and the image reserves 9121 for the admin listener, which opens only when `admin_port` is set.

Setting `enable_lifecycle` registers the lifecycle-subscriber protocol on the same gRPC port. On the Postgres producer, `enable_executor` registers an executor and its observability sibling there too; its attribute contract is below.

### Sensors

Each sensor implements the publisher protocol on one gRPC port and calls the control API to publish messages.

| Image | gRPC port | Other listener |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `rimsky-sensor-cron` | 9081 | — |
| `rimsky-sensor-http` | 9082 | — |
| `rimsky-sensor-object-store` | 9083 | — |
| `rimsky-sensor-webhook` | 9084 | HTTP ingress on 9184 |

Every sensor takes its host and port from its own namespaced pair, `RIMSKY_SENSOR_<NAME>_HOST` and `RIMSKY_SENSOR_<NAME>_PORT`, and finds the orchestrator at `RIMSKY_CONTROL_API_URL`, defaulting to `http://localhost:8080`. `sensor-webhook` takes its ingress port from `RIMSKY_SENSOR_WEBHOOK_HTTP_PORT`.

Every sensor takes an optional `RIMSKY_SENSOR_<NAME>_STATE_DSN`. The four share one shape and one engine: a `postgres://` URL. One Postgres instance backs all four, each bootstrapping its own table in it, and no two sensors share a table. Leave the variable unset and the sensor runs stateless. Set it to a host that does not resolve and the sensor exits non-zero naming its state database, rather than falling back to stateless.

Two replicas of a sensor give failover without duplicate messages. The control API mounts each subscription on exactly one replica, so the second is a cold spare; stopping the holder hands the subscription to the survivor with no scheduled window skipped. Should both replicas ever hold the same watch, both fire the same window under the same idempotency key and the instance still receives exactly one message.

`sensor-http` dials poll targets through a default-closed egress guard, described below. `sensor-object-store` registers a filesystem backend when `RIMSKY_SENSOR_OBJECT_STORE_FS_ROOT` names a directory, and an in-process memory backend when `RIMSKY_SENSOR_OBJECT_STORE_ENABLE_MEMORY_BACKEND=1`. Those two are the whole set — the build services no cloud object store. A publisher declaring `backend: s3`, `gcs`, or `azure` never leaves `mounting`, and the reason appears only in the orchestrator's log: the backend is not serviceable by this build. Under the filesystem backend, a bucket is a subdirectory of the operator's own root.

`sensor-webhook` answers `GET /health` on its ingress port. It also enforces the `auth` block a webhook publisher declares — a delivery without the credential gets 401, and a webhook publisher that declares no `auth` block never mounts at all. An HTTP-poll publisher accepts the same `auth` block at registration and at deploy, mounts live, and then polls the upstream without those credentials. Nothing warns. Present credentials to a poll target another way.

### Executors

| Image | gRPC port | HTTP port |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `rimsky-executor-http-node` | 9091 | 9092 |
| `rimsky-executor-claude-agent` | 9090 | 9190 |
| `rimsky-executor-verifier-shape-checks` | 9095 | — |
| `rimsky-executor-verifier-http` | 9096 | — |

All four take `RIMSKY_EXECUTOR_HOST` (default `0.0.0.0`) and `RIMSKY_EXECUTOR_PORT_GRPC`. `http-node` and `claude-agent` take `RIMSKY_EXECUTOR_PORT_HTTP` as well; `http-node` defaults it to one above its gRPC port, and opens it always. The two verifier images open no HTTP listener and their Dockerfiles publish no port, so map their gRPC ports explicitly.

`rimsky-executor-claude-agent` spawns the Claude Code CLI as a subprocess, so its runtime carries a real userland — a shell and git — rather than the static base the other images use. The CLI binary is pinned at build time. The executor starts only when it finds a Claude credential in its environment or runs in stub mode; otherwise it exits naming the two credential variables it accepts. `RIMSKY_EXECUTOR_CLAUDE_BINARY` overrides the CLI path. `RIMSKY_EXECUTOR_SILENCE_MS` and `RIMSKY_EXECUTOR_TOOL_USE_TIMEOUT_MS` set the per-dispatch defaults a node may override. `RIMSKY_DISPATCH_MAX_USD` caps a dispatch's spend.

Two allowlists bound what a node may ask the Claude executor for: `RIMSKY_CLAUDE_AGENT_MCP_ALLOWLIST` over the MCP servers a node declares, and `RIMSKY_CLAUDE_AGENT_EXPOSE_ENV_ALLOWLIST` over the environment names a node exposes to the agent. Both are comma-separated. **Unset means open, not closed.** With the MCP allowlist unset, a node's declared server runs; with the expose-env allowlist unset, a node reads any variable it names from the container's environment. Set them to an exact boundary and a node naming anything outside it fails that dispatch with an error naming the entry, the instance, and the node.

### Subscriber

**`rimsky-subscriber-openlineage`** exports rimsky's lineage records to an OpenLineage backend. It opens no port. It polls rimsky's lineage table over `RIMSKY_OPENLINEAGE_RIMSKY_DSN` — a `postgres://` or `postgresql://` URL, and it refuses anything else, so it has no export path for a SQLite-backed deployment — and posts events to `RIMSKY_OPENLINEAGE_BACKEND_URL`. Both are required. `RIMSKY_OPENLINEAGE_STATE_DSN` holds its own cursor and defaults to the rimsky DSN. `RIMSKY_OPENLINEAGE_BEARER_TOKEN`, `RIMSKY_OPENLINEAGE_NAMESPACE` (default `rimsky`), `RIMSKY_OPENLINEAGE_POLL_INTERVAL` (default 5s), `RIMSKY_OPENLINEAGE_BATCH_SIZE` (default 200), and `RIMSKY_OPENLINEAGE_LAG_WINDOW` (default 2s) tune the rest.

## Ports

| Port | Listener |
| --- | --- |
| 8080 | Control API |
| 9081 | `sensor-cron` gRPC |
| 9082 | `sensor-http` gRPC |
| 9083 | `sensor-object-store` gRPC |
| 9084 | `sensor-webhook` gRPC |
| 9090 | `claude-agent` gRPC |
| 9090 | `host-agent-proxy` agent-facing gRPC |
| 9091 | `http-node` gRPC |
| 9091 | `host-agent-proxy` peer-facing mTLS gRPC |
| 9092 | `http-node` HTTP |
| 9095 | `verifier-shape-checks` gRPC |
| 9096 | `verifier-http` gRPC |
| 9100 | `claim-producer-filesystem` gRPC |
| 9100 | Supervisor async-callback listener, as baked into `rimsky-all-in-one` |
| 9101 | `claim-producer-postgres` gRPC |
| 9110 | `claim-producer-filesystem` HTTP bridge |
| 9111 | `claim-producer-postgres` HTTP bridge |
| 9121 | `claim-producer-postgres` admin |
| 9184 | `sensor-webhook` HTTP ingress |
| 9190 | `claude-agent` HTTP |

**Three of these defaults collide when the whole bundle shares one network namespace.** The filesystem claim producer's 9100 is the port the supervisor's callback listener already holds, and the host-agent proxy's 9090 is the Claude executor's gRPC port. Each collision is between a service and a core listener rather than between two services, which is where an operator reading per-service defaults would not look. Both are configuration away: give the filesystem producer a `grpc_port` and `http_port` of your own, or move the proxy with `RIMSKY_PROXY_GRPC_PORT`. The other nine services share the namespace at their defaults without complaint.

## Executor attribute contracts

Each executor image reads a set of attributes from the node it runs and returns an attributes delta the runtime merges back into that node. This section names both halves per image.

### `http-node`

Reads `url` (required), `method` (default `GET`), `headers`, `body`, `expect_status`, and `error_class_field`.

When the node declares no `body`, the executor sends every attribute outside that configuration set as the JSON request body. So a node's ordinary inputs become the request payload without being named twice.

Writes back the response. A JSON object body becomes the attributes delta whole. A non-JSON body becomes `body_base64` and `content_type`. The change summary carries the status and the URL, and the outcome is marked changed.

A 429 with an unexpected status parks the node, taking the resume instant from the response's `Retry-After` header. An unexpected status returns an error class read from the response's `error_class_field`, defaulting to `error_class` and overridable per node.

Stub mode adds six more keys: `stub_probe`, `stub_response`, `stub_tags`, `probe_park`, `probe_cancel`, and `park_resume_at`. They govern only when the operator has set `RIMSKY_EXECUTOR_STUB_MODE=1` on the executor process.

### `claude-agent`

Reads `cwd_from_claim_producer`, `cwd`, `model` (default `claude-sonnet-4-5`), `system_prompt`, `user_prompt`, `session_token` (read-only — the executor writes it), and a `cli` object.

The `cli` object takes `bare`, `allowed_tools`, `disallowed_tools`, `add_dirs`, `max_budget_usd`, `permission_mode` (`default`, `acceptEdits`, `bypassPermissions`, or `plan`), `max_schema_corrections` (default 3), `handle_rate_limits` (default true), `expose_env`, `mcp_servers`, `required_signoffs`, `max_signoff_attempts` (default 3), `silence_timeout_ms`, and `tool_use_timeout_ms`.

Each `mcp_servers` entry names a `name` and a `transport`, and the rest of its keys follow from the transport. An `http` entry takes `url`, optional `headers`, and optional `allowed_tools`. A `stdio` entry takes `command`, optional `args`, optional `env`, and optional `allowed_tools`. A `module` entry — `http-loopback` is an accepted spelling of the same transport — takes `module` and optional `allowed_tools`.

Each `required_signoffs` entry takes a `public_key` and an optional `path`.

The schema accepts additional properties, so a node may carry its own inputs and outputs beside these keys.

Writes back whatever the agent reports as its completion delta, with `session_token` always set to the run's session identifier. The agent's own reported change flag and change summary come back with it. Resume a later run against the same session by passing that token back in `session_token`.

### `verifier-http`

Reads `url` (required), `timeout_ms` (default 60000), `expected_status`, `body`, and `class_field` (default `class`). It POSTs the JSON-encoded `body` to the URL.

Writes back `verifier_pass: true` and `verifier_status`, the response status, marked unchanged. An unexpected status returns error class `verifier/check_failed`, extended with the upstream class read from `class_field` when the response carries one, and a payload holding `actual_status`, `expected_status`, and a body preview.

### `verifier-shape-checks`

Reads `checks` (a non-empty array, required) and `rows` (an array of objects). Each check takes `kind`, `config`, and `severity` — `error` or `warning`, defaulting to `error`. Eight kinds ship: `no_nulls`, `nullable_fields_present`, `pk_unique`, `row_count_ratio`, `row_count_absolute`, `value_in_set`, `regex_match`, and `numeric_range`. All but the two row-count kinds need `rows`, and the executor fails the dispatch naming the check when `rows` is absent.

A template may bind `checks` from a `source` rather than declare it as a literal default. The image's validation service enforces one or the other at template registration.

Writes back `verifier_pass: true`, `verifier_checks`, `verifier_rows`, `verifier_warning_count`, and `verifier_warnings`, marked unchanged. A failing check at `error` severity returns error class `verifier/check_failed/<kind>` with a payload holding `failures`, `warnings`, and a summary. A malformed check configuration returns `verifier/attribute_invalid`.

### `claim-producer-postgres` under `enable_executor`

Reads `schema`, `table`, and `checks`, each check taking `kind` and `config`. Four kinds run: `no_nulls`, `row_count_absolute`, `row_count_ratio`, and `pk_unique`. It runs them as SQL against the named table rather than over row data the node carries.

Writes back `verifier_pass: true`, `verifier_checks`, and a `results` array of per-check `kind`, `pass`, and counts, marked unchanged. A failing check returns error class `pg/verifier_check_failed/<kind>` with a failures payload. Bad attributes return `pg/attribute_invalid`, and a lost connection pool returns `pg/connection_lost`.

## What these images do not do

Seven expectations the shipped set does not meet. Each is worth knowing before you write a deployment around it.

**No bundled service exposes metrics.** The three core roles each serve Prometheus text on a separate metrics listener, opened by `RIMSKY_METRICS_PORT` and the per-role variables beside it. The control API's own port answers 404 there — the metrics listener is its own port, not a route on the API. Carrying the same variables to any of the eleven bundled services opens nothing: no service declares a metrics port, none answers on any port it does open, and the OpenLineage subscriber opens no port at all. Dashboards cover the three core roles and nothing else.

**No bundled service honors the log level.** The core process and the host-agent proxy both read `RIMSKY_LOG_LEVEL`, and all eleven bundled services fix their level at info and ignore it. The accepted values are `debug`, `warn`, and `error`. Anything else — a capitalized `DEBUG`, a borrowed `trace` — falls back to info silently, with the offending value named nowhere.

**One HTTP liveness path is not enough.** Three listeners in the shipped set answer an HTTP health route: the control API at `GET /v1/health`, the supervisor's callback listener at `GET /health`, and `sensor-webhook`'s ingress at `GET /health`. The rest either spell it differently or serve no HTTP at all. One probe specification applied to every rimsky container fails on most of them.

**Stub mode is per-executor, not a platform feature.** Every bundled executor's schema accepts `stub_response`, and three different things happen at dispatch. `http-node` honors it and settles with the author's object as the delta. `claude-agent` honors it only when the node also sets `stub_probe: true`. `verifier-http` ignores it and settles with its own canned marker. `verifier-shape-checks` does not stub at all and fails asking for the real row data its check needs. None of them honors it unless the operator set `RIMSKY_EXECUTOR_STUB_MODE=1` on the executor process — without that flag, an ordinary `http-node` makes the real request. The park controls behave the same way: `probe_park`, `probe_cancel`, and `park_resume_at` register cleanly on every executor and reach a parked node on `http-node` and `claude-agent` only, in stub mode only. A template author cannot exercise a graph offline by declaring these attributes.

**The SSRF guard covers two outbound dialers, not all of them.** `http-node` and `sensor-http` dial through a default-closed egress guard: it blocks loopback, private, link-local — including the cloud metadata address — unique-local, and multicast destinations, checked on the resolved IP at connect time so redirects and DNS rebinding are covered, and it restricts the scheme to HTTP and HTTPS. Reopen a range with `RIMSKY_EXECUTOR_HTTP_NODE_EGRESS_ALLOWLIST` or `RIMSKY_SENSOR_HTTP_EGRESS_ALLOWLIST`, comma-separated CIDRs or addresses, parsed at startup — a malformed entry fails the boot. Nothing else is behind it. `verifier-http` takes its `url` from node attributes exactly as `http-node` does, reaches a private address, and has no allowlist variable at all. The OpenLineage subscriber posts to whatever URL it is configured with, the metadata address included. The Claude executor hands node-declared MCP server URLs to the CLI unexamined.

Note the polarity difference between the two allowlist families, because they share a naming style and point opposite ways. An unset `_EGRESS_ALLOWLIST` allows nothing private. An unset `RIMSKY_CLAUDE_AGENT_*_ALLOWLIST` allows everything — that is the open configuration a zero-configuration local stack runs on.

**Migration runs forward only.** The entrypoint applies migrations, and re-running is safe: a second container over the same state directory applies nothing and comes up healthy. There is no rollback. `RIMSKY_ENTRYPOINT_MIGRATE` accepts `1`, `0`, and unset, and refuses anything else; no CLI verb runs migrations; and every driver applies its numbered migrations in one direction. An upgrade runbook has nothing to call for a downgrade step. The migrate binary ships in the image and exits when it finishes, so a one-shot init container reaches it by replacing the image's entrypoint — the entrypoint's own role argument does not name it, and `RIMSKY_ENTRYPOINT_MIGRATE=1` migrates and then serves a role rather than finishing.

**Most protocols are gRPC only.** The claim-producer protocol speaks HTTP+JSON on the bridge ports, and the conformance runner drives it there. The executor bridge ports carry an HTTP+JSON execute path, and rimsky dispatches over it when an executor is configured with the HTTP transport. Every other protocol — validation, data processing, publisher, lifecycle subscriber, host agent — is gRPC only, and the conformance runner refuses any transport but gRPC for them. Pointing a claim producer's configured endpoint at its own HTTP bridge stops the stack; the endpoint scheme must be `grpc://`.
